newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean police enter German enclave, then leave.
newsitem.headline: Chilean police enter German enclave, then leave.

text.p: Chilean police entered and later retreated from a secretive German settlement in southern Chile for a brief inspection on Tuesday, and a top official said a raid to arrest its fugitive leader could follow.

A convoy of police vans and trucks passed the first gate of Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) but stopped short of an inner gate leading into the shadowy community's living areas, where founder Paul Schaeffer, wanted on child abuse and other charges, may be holed up.
Under a steady drizzle, most of the contingent later turned back to park at the community's edge in an operation that police on the scene called a "visual inspection."
But a handful of officers was allowed past the inner gate and inspected some buildings, Megavision TV network reported.
"I cannot allow you to enter. You may not enter," an elderly man at the colony's inner gate told police in Spanish in a thick German accent.

"Yes, we will enter. We have a prosecutor's instructions for a visual inspection, that's all," said a police inspector, in a tense dialogue shown by Megavision. The inspectors left after four hours, while scores more waited outside.
Police commander Julio Poo told reporters the purpose of the visit was "to carry out a visual inspection. It is not a raid...We have come to gather information."

Church bells rang out inside the colony, and residents lit a huge bonfire, apparently signalling their fears of a raid on the secluded community, where a few hundred German-speaking residents live behind barbed-wire fences.

Schaeffer, a balding German man believed to be in his 80s who has been charged with molesting boys, was presumed to be hiding inside the sprawling estate in the Andean foothills near the town of Parral, 200 miles (320 km) south of Santiago.

He issued a blistering statement last week saying he feared for his life and would not get a fair trial in Chile if he surrendered. His lawyers quit after the statement, saying they had tried to persuade him to give himself up.

Two confidants, both German citizens, and two Chilean members of the settlement surrendered to police last week to face charges including the illegal detention of a child, obstruction of justice and the destruction of public property. All four were later released on bail.

Schaeffer set up the colony in the mid-1950s. It was protected by the former military regime of Gen. Augusto Pinochet, and human rights groups have charged that the military used it as a secret detention and torture centre.

A special prosecutor appointed by President Eduardo Frei's government issued an arrest warrant for Schaeffer last year on charges that he molested at least five Chilean boys whose parents had sent them to a boarding school in the community.
In Santiago, Interior Minister Carlos Figueroa said officials were not sure if Schaeffer was inside the colony but police had warrants to storm the place if given the order.

"The arrest order (for Schaeffer) calls for the possibility of proceeding to raiding the place and forcing open its locks in case that's necessary," Figueroa said. "The police are fully allowed to do that."
The child abuse charges alienated the colony's one-time allies among conservative Chilean politicians and the Roman Catholic Church, who have urged Schaeffer to give himself up.
Allies of the government ridiculed the police inspection, saying it would only signal weakness to the fugitive inside.

"They were practically asking Paul Schaeffer for an invitation to visit. This is a joke and an outrage, and a clear demonstration that the authorities do not want to investigate what is going on inside Colonia Dignidad," said a left-wing member of Congress, Jaime Naranjo.
Naranjo and other congressmen suggested police were under pressure not to dig too deeply for Schaeffer, who is reported to have good contacts in the Chilean military.

Adding to the tension, a Chilean cameraman for a German television crew was bashed on the head by one of the colony's security men on Sunday while he was filming the colony from a nearby hillside, and he suffered a mild concussion.
The attack was strongly condemned by local politicians and news media and the Chilean Foreign Press Association.
A few elderly German women residents said at the settlement's gates on Monday night that police were persecuting them and they had not seen Schaeffer in months.
"We came to Chile for peace, and we don't know why we are being subjected to this. It is so unfair," one woman said, speaking in German and looking distraught.
